cells.tense: You are steering from here, hands on the wheel, with only part of the road in view.
cells.act: hold your shape under the weight
cells.ask: Pick one open question you're carrying — a decision, an answer you're waiting on — and skip trying to settle it for a week. Keep driving. Notice whether you can carry something undecided without tightening around it.
cells.core:
You're directing something, and today the direction comes from what's actually here rather than from what you're braced against. One step is visible; the whole road isn't. You're using the step anyway, which is why the choice reads as chosen rather than forced, and why you can still stand behind it in the morning.

The way this holds is endurance without gripping. Choose one question you're carrying and stop working it toward a resolution for the next week — don't solve it early, don't walk away from it. See whether your course continues while the question sits undecided. Carrying something open without clenching around it is the whole practice; if you can, the decision stays yours, and if you can't, you learn that sooner than you might have.

cells.verb: say 'this, not that,' and mean it

cells.tense: You are already living inside an outcome that hasn't happened yet, and steering hard at it.
cells.act: draw the whole arrangement you are inside, with yourself marked on it
cells.ask: Pick a situation you're pushing toward an outcome and draw it — the whole arrangement, you included. Not the plan you want; the thing as it stands. Put the drawing where you'll see it before your next move.
cells.core:
You're steering toward a future already cast in your head, and the steering has gone tight. From inside it feels like focus — you're just being decisive — but the decisions keep aiming at events that haven't arrived, and reality keeps not matching the script. Something in your shoulders braces when you think about it.

There's a reason the pattern doesn't feel like control from where you stand: you're trying to stay ahead of something, which is a different motion and a tiring one. Try looking instead of pushing. Draw one situation, the whole arrangement, with yourself marked on it — once, this week. What's actually there tends to show itself, and the forcing has somewhere to set down. You'll see where you are in it, not only where you're shoving.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door already behind you, and the handle left your hand a long time ago.
cells.act: do one thing today the way only you do it, and do not explain it
cells.ask: Make today's tea, or walk your usual route, or answer a message — your manner, no explanation offered, no reason attached. Then leave it alone. Nothing more is asked of you today.
cells.core:
You recall what deciding felt like, and it isn't happening now. Instead there's drift with momentum, and 'what's the point' is the sound of that drift. You still show up, but you aren't aimed anywhere, and tomorrow reads like fog the whole way down. The thing in you that says 'this, not that' isn't gone — it's starved, and starved, it pushes effort into the wrong places.

What refills it comes through something you are, not something you push harder at. So today, do one ordinary act your own way and don't explain it. Not toward a goal, not for anyone's notice. Your manner shows up in the doing, and small as that is, the next ordinary act tends to get its direction back.

cells.tense: You are drifting with momentum and calling it habit, though the motion is run by you.
cells.act: put your own name on what is already yours
cells.ask: When a routine you keep starts running without you deciding it, tell yourself right then that you keep it because you chose to. Say it plainly once. Do that each time you catch it, and change nothing else.
cells.core:
You're steering something, and the direction is in your hands, but your own account of it leaves your hands out. The momentum feels like habit or circumstance, and that's the word you use even alone. Seen from outside, the pattern is plain: you are choosing, and you are describing it as drift. Only the description is off.

This week, try naming. When a routine you keep runs, tell yourself that it's yours — attach your own name to the activity you're in. Nothing changes in the activity; what changes is who gets the credit for it in your own story. That's the whole move, and it's repeatable: each time you notice it running, the direction lands back on the record.
